questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities, i.e. the classes the host university could provide. Also personal connection to the destination and exploring new cultures as I have been wanting to try out living in the UK for a long time and this seemed like a good opportunity to try out both. I also wanted to strengthen my English.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had trouble with getting the classes I wanted. I ended up liking the classes I got in the end, but would still have preferred to be without the initial trouble and still also would have liked to partake in the classes they told me I couldn't register for.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Fairly easy, I did not have too much trouble with that initially. What I would have liked to know prior to even applying was that some modules would not be available for me as an exchange student. That was sadly the majority that I wanted when I applied, and nobody made me aware of it before I was on campus for welcome week.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: University staff drove me to my private accommodation with my luggage for free after arriving in Exeter by a (self paid) bus arranged by university to go from Heathrow Airport to campus. I also used the drop in sessions to figure out what was happening with my modules.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: The international welcome team was very accommodating with drop in sessions throughout the first few weeks.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I used the portal provided by the university as well as websites that the university had recommended. Apply for a lot of places as the UK housing market is in general pretty bad. I ended up having two interviews, and got them both offered, but also didn't hear back from many. Some landlords prefer that you stay for a full year, but short term is possible. I loved where I ended up living: With my English landlady and her teenage son, and two other study abroad students who were also doing a semester abroad as part of their postgraduate.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
Exeter is quite hilly but you can walk anywhere. Before going I thought I'd get a bike, but I ended up deciding not to because the infrastructure for bikes isn't the best, and then also the hills. I had a 30-40 minute walk to campus, but could go by public transportation if the weather was bad. I love walking and enjoyed the trip back and forth. I used it to make phone calls to people from home, or I walked with friends or housemates.

Housing in Exeter is not as good as in Copenhagen, albeit it's as (or more) expensive. Pack some wool as it can get cold indoors. I have friends who lived in moldy student houses or even had slugs indoors. I did not have any of that, but the conditions of the houses can be pretty bad. My study abroad friends typically lived in either private dorms or student houses with 4-9 people. Some lived with families.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I did not meet any study abroad term 1 students who got accommodation through the university. They cannot guarantee housing in their dorms if you're only there for the autumn semester.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I thought the registration process was fairly easy when I did it. But then, after arrival, I got to learn that most of the modules I had applied for were not available to me as a study abroad student.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I sent a module "wish list" in June, I think. I think I had to apply for 6 or 8 classes. Then I got my final modules after arrival, and then you could also try to change modules within the first few weeks if you did not get what you wanted.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I don't remember what was available when I applied at home, but on campus they had drop in sessions every day for the first few weeks of term for international students.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Somewhat. I got some classes that were good in the end, but I had applied for UoE for some specific courses in curation that I ended up not being allowed to take. I was quite disappointed by that as it did not say it anywhere beforehand. Then UoE assigned me for another class, and then a few days later contacted me saying that I could not get that class even though they had already registered me in it and because it was a mandatory course for an MA. I ended up being in another mandatory MA module at another programme, so I don't know why that one wasn't a problem. I did get one module that was high on my priority list.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Make sure to check if the classes you want are actually eligible for exchange students. I don't know how though as they do not write it explicitly if a module is not.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: It was kind of similar to UCPH but in some ways a bit lower. During presentations people were allowed to read out loud from their papers/computers which would not be the case in DK. I had a lot of readings for my classes but around the same as . I think it also depends a lot on the modules/programme you study, as some of my business student friends in Exeter did not have much reading to do but instead many classes.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
It felt very similar to what I have been used to at UCPH. The classes were small (typical for MA in humanities in Exeter), but so are mine at UCPH. In "Cultures of Creativity" we did some more experimental things, but that reminded me of my BA that I studied at The Danish School of Media and Journalism (DMJX).

Examination is different at UoE than UCPH. I did not have any specific end of term exams. Instead, they comprised of different tasks throughout the term, and all the credits got put together for one grade per module. My final credit/grade was made of the following:
Intercultural Communication: 50% essay, 25% group presentation, 25% video cast (video recording of a presentation)
Cultures of Creativity: 50% digital portfolio, 50% essay

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
DRAM143 Cultures of Creativity (15 ECTS)
SMLM087 Intercultural Communication: Key Concepts and Theories (15 ECTS)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Both were good. In "Cultures of Creativity" I got to be creative and reflect on my own practice as a well as discussing the pros and cons of the creative industries. "Intercultural Communication" was interesting to do in an international setting.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Transfer fees from my bank when paying rent. I also spent a lot on "personal spending" but that includes all clothes, trips to Boots, trips around the UK, cultural and social activities.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Books. I got access to all study materials through the university library.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: All kinds. They have +100 different societies ranging from hide and seek to sports to photography to Taylor Swift.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: They host "international cafes" where you can get a free pastry and hot beverage which is a nice way to meet other internationals too. Pub quizzes are a lot of fun. And join some societies if you feel like it.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Do go on trips! I went on many train trips with friends. We used our reading week to take an 8 hour train to Edinburgh directly from Exeter which I would really recommend. Do look into getting a youth train pass (you can buy it in the Trainline app) as it's quickly gained if you plan to travel by train just a bit. I went to Edinburgh, Glasgow, Manchester, London, Bristol and Lynmouth for overnight stays. For one day trips I did Plymouth, Exmouth, St. Ives, Sidmouth, Bath – and my studies didn't suffer. I'd recommend them all. The national park Dartmoor is amazing too!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I did not have any troubles with that.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I mainly spent time with other international students, as there was also more international than local students in my classes (which is pretty common for MA modules).

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I did not find anything particularly challenging as I think Danes and the Brits have quite similar manners. The locals do drink a lot though. And the cashier might call you "love" or "darling", but that's just a sweet gesture.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Cream tea and the good chips with cheddar and vinegar. They are also more open/small talk more with strangers than Danes, I'd say.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1: Participate in the welcome things that UoE has planned: They do a lot and you'll definitely meet some sweet people there. Just go, even if you're going alone - you'll find your people, even if you are a late 20's student like me and not an 18 year old fresher.
2: Make sure you are eligible for the classes you really want. Perhaps double check with UoE before you go if they are very important for you.
3: Do go on all the little trips your heart desires with the people you meet. It's great fun to see more of the UK that isn't London. And the train ride to Scotland was actually nice as you cross through so much of the UK on the way.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Not that I can think of right now.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The people I've met, places I've seen and getting back a photography spark. I've also gotten ideas for my thesis through my courses.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The UK being expensive and wanting to do everything. Do try to apply for scholarships, I did get one from Augustinusfonden.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
